steps.text: Often a function is known only at individual points: from measurements, from a table, or because each evaluation is an expensive simulation. Example – three measured values:
steps.explanation:
What is the value at \(x = 1.5\)? Nothing was measured there.

The idea of interpolation: look for a simple function \(p\) that passes exactly through all given points, and then evaluate \(p\) at the desired point.

The given \(x\) values are called nodes, the \(y\) values data values.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Values between the data points
steps.insight: Interpolation: find a function that passes exactly through all given points.

steps.text: Why polynomials? They have many practical properties:
steps.explanation:
• They are easy to evaluate – only additions and multiplications.
• They are easy to differentiate and integrate.
• By the Weierstrass theorem, every continuous function on an interval can be approximated arbitrarily well by polynomials.

Interpolating polynomials are also a tool for other methods: Simpson's rule for numerical integration and many methods for differential equations arise by replacing the function with an interpolating polynomial.

Our roadmap:
1. Existence and uniqueness
2. Three forms: monomials, Lagrange, Newton
3. Neville's scheme for quick evaluation
4. The interpolation error
5. Why high degrees are dangerous – and how Chebyshev nodes help
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Values between the data points
steps.insight: Polynomials are easy to handle – and the basis of many numerical methods.

steps.text: Interpolation is not the same as least squares fitting:
steps.explanation:
• Interpolation: the function passes exactly through all points. Sensible when the values are exact (tables, exact function values).

• Least squares (lesson “Least Squares & QR Decomposition”): the function passes as close as possible to the points, but not necessarily through them. Sensible for noisy measurements.

In interpolation the polynomial has as many parameters as there are points. In least squares it has fewer.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Values between the data points
steps.insight: Interpolation: exactly through the points. Least squares: as close as possible.

steps.text: How many points are needed for which polynomial? Through two points passes exactly one line (degree 1). Through three points passes exactly one parabola (degree 2). In general:
steps.formula: \text{For } n + 1 \text{ points } (x_0, y_0), \ldots, (x_n, y_n) \text{ with distinct } x_i \text{ there is exactly one polynomial } p \text{ of degree} \le n \text{ with } p(x_i) = y_i
steps.explanation:
A polynomial of degree \(\le n\) has \(n + 1\) coefficients: \(p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + \ldots + a_n x^n\). Each point gives one condition – \(n + 1\) conditions for \(n + 1\) unknowns fits exactly.

Careful: “degree \(\le n\)”, not “degree \(= n\)”. If three points happen to lie on a line, the interpolating polynomial is this line (degree 1).
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Exactly one polynomial
steps.insight: \(n + 1\) points ⇒ exactly one interpolating polynomial of degree \(\le n\).

steps.text: The direct way: ansatz \(p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2\) and plug in the three points:
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Exactly one polynomial
steps.insight: Monomial ansatz: determine the coefficients from a linear system.

steps.text: The linear system of the monomial ansatz has a special matrix, the Vandermonde matrix:
steps.formula: V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_0 & x_0^2 & \cdots & x_0^n \\ 1 & x_1 & x_1^2 & \cdots & x_1^n \\ \vdots & & & & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & x_n^2 & \cdots & x_n^n \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
It is invertible if all \(x_i\) are distinct – which proves existence.

Uniqueness can also be seen directly: if \(p\) and \(q\) were two interpolating polynomials of degree \(\le n\), then \(p - q\) would have the \(n + 1\) roots \(x_0, \ldots, x_n\). But a polynomial of degree \(\le n\) with more than \(n\) roots is the zero polynomial, so \(p = q\).

Numerically the Vandermonde matrix is unfortunately a problem: its condition number grows extremely fast with \(n\) (for 20 equally spaced points on \([0, 1]\) far above \(10^{10}\)). The columns \(x^k\) look more and more alike for large \(k\). That is why other representations are used.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Exactly one polynomial
steps.insight: Monomial ansatz: simple, but ill-conditioned for many points. The Lagrange and Newton forms are better.

steps.text: Quick check: determine the interpolating polynomial through \((1, 2)\) and \((3, 8)\). What is its value at \(x = 2\)?
steps.explanation:
Two points, so a line \(p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x\).
• Slope: \(a_1 = \frac{8 - 2}{3 - 1} = 3\)
• \(p(1) = a_0 + 3 = 2 \Rightarrow a_0 = -1\)

\(p(x) = 3x - 1\), \(p(2) = 5\) – exactly the mean of \(2\) and \(8\), as expected for linear interpolation in the middle.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Exactly one polynomial
steps.insight: Linear interpolation is the simplest case: the line through two points.

steps.text: Lagrange had an elegant idea: for each point build a “switch polynomial” \(L_i\) that is \(1\) at its own node and \(0\) at all other nodes:
steps.explanation:
Once you have such polynomials, interpolation is trivial:
\(p(x) = y_0 L_0(x) + y_1 L_1(x) + \ldots + y_n L_n(x)\)

Why? Plug in \(x = x_j\): all \(L_i\) with \(i \neq j\) are \(0\) there, only \(L_j(x_j) = 1\). So \(p(x_j) = y_j\) ✓

The \(L_i\) are called Lagrange basis polynomials.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · The Lagrange form
steps.insight: Lagrange's idea: basis polynomials that are 1 at exactly one node and 0 at all others.

steps.text: How do you construct \(L_0\) for the nodes \(0, 1, 2\)? It must vanish at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\) – so it contains the factors \((x - 1)\) and \((x - 2)\):
steps.explanation:
The numerator provides the roots at \(1\) and \(2\). The denominator is the same expression evaluated at \(x = 0\) – that makes \(L_0(0) = 1\).

In the same way:
• \(L_1(x) = \frac{(x - 0)(x - 2)}{(1 - 0)(1 - 2)} = -x(x - 2)\)
• \(L_2(x) = \frac{(x - 0)(x - 1)}{(2 - 0)(2 - 1)} = \frac{x(x - 1)}{2}\)

Check for \(L_1\): \(L_1(0) = 0\) ✓, \(L_1(1) = -1 \cdot (-1) = 1\) ✓, \(L_1(2) = 0\) ✓
steps.section: Chapter 3 · The Lagrange form
steps.insight: \(L_i\): numerator = product of all \((x - x_j)\) with \(j \neq i\), denominator = the same at \(x = x_i\).

steps.text: Now the interpolating polynomial for \(y = (1, 3, 2)\):
steps.explanation:
The animation shows the three weighted basis polynomials and their sum.

Evaluating at \(x = 1.5\):
• \(L_0(1.5) = \frac{0.5 \cdot (-0.5)}{2} = -0.125\)
• \(L_1(1.5) = -1.5 \cdot (-0.5) = 0.75\)
• \(L_2(1.5) = \frac{1.5 \cdot 0.5}{2} = 0.375\)

\(p(1.5) = 1 \cdot (-0.125) + 3 \cdot 0.75 + 2 \cdot 0.375 = -0.125 + 2.25 + 0.75 = 2.875\) ✓

The same as with the monomial ansatz – it is the same polynomial, just written differently.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · The Lagrange form
steps.insight: Lagrange form: \(p(x) = \sum_i y_i L_i(x)\). No linear system needed.

steps.text: In general the Lagrange form reads:
steps.formula: p(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} y_i\, L_i(x), \qquad L_i(x) = \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j}
steps.explanation:
Advantages:
• It can be written down immediately, without solving a linear system.
• It nicely shows that \(p\) depends linearly on the values \(y_i\).
• It is good for theoretical considerations (for example deriving integration formulas).

Disadvantages:
• Each evaluation costs about \(n^2\) operations.
• If a new point is added, all basis polynomials change – everything has to be recomputed.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · The Lagrange form
steps.insight: Lagrange: ideal for theory and small examples. Impractical when points are added.

steps.text: Quick check: the basis polynomials satisfy \(\sum_i L_i(x) = 1\) for all \(x\). Why?
steps.explanation:
Interpolate the constant function \(f(x) = 1\), i.e. all \(y_i = 1\). By Lagrange the interpolating polynomial is \(\sum_i 1 \cdot L_i(x)\).

But the function \(1\) is itself a polynomial of degree \(0 \le n\) passing through all points. By uniqueness, \(\sum_i L_i(x) = 1\).

Check at \(x = 1.5\): \(-0.125 + 0.75 + 0.375 = 1\) ✓
steps.section: Chapter 3 · The Lagrange form
steps.insight: The Lagrange basis polynomials always sum to 1.

steps.text: The Newton form builds up the polynomial point by point. The ansatz for three points:
steps.explanation:
The trick: at \(x = x_0\) all terms except \(c_0\) vanish, at \(x = x_1\) all from the third on. So the coefficients can be determined one after another.

For \((0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2)\):
• \(x = 0\): \(p(0) = c_0 = 1\)
• \(x = 1\): \(p(1) = 1 + c_1 \cdot 1 = 3 \Rightarrow c_1 = 2\)
• \(x = 2\): \(p(2) = 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + c_2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 2 \Rightarrow c_2 = -1.5\)

\(p(x) = 1 + 2x - 1.5\,x(x - 1)\). Multiplied out: \(1 + 3.5x - 1.5x^2\) ✓
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The Newton form and divided differences
steps.insight: Newton form: determine the coefficients one after another – a triangular system instead of a full one.

steps.text: The coefficients of the Newton form are the divided differences. They are defined recursively:
steps.explanation:
In words: a divided difference is “the difference of the two shorter divided differences, divided by the distance between the outermost nodes”.

The first divided difference \(f[x_i, x_{i+1}]\) is simply the slope of the secant. The second is something like a “slope of the slopes” – related to the second derivative.

Then: \(c_k = f[x_0, \ldots, x_k]\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The Newton form and divided differences
steps.insight: Divided differences: difference of the two shorter ones divided by the distance between the outermost nodes.

steps.text: The computation is arranged in the divided difference table. For our example:
steps.explanation:
How to read the table:
• Column 2: the given \(y\) values.
• Column 3: two neighbouring values from column 2 – difference divided by the distance of the \(x\) values.
• Column 4: two neighbouring values from column 3 – difference divided by the distance of the outermost \(x\) values (\(2 - 0\)).

The bold numbers on the upper diagonal are the Newton coefficients: \(c_0 = 1\), \(c_1 = 2\), \(c_2 = -1.5\) ✓
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The Newton form and divided differences
steps.insight: In the table, the Newton coefficients are on the upper diagonal.

steps.text: The big advantage of the Newton form: if a point is added, only one diagonal row has to be appended. New point \((3, 5)\):
steps.explanation:
Only the bottom diagonal row was newly computed: \(3\), then \(2\), then \(\frac{7}{6}\).

The new polynomial:
\(p_3(x) = \underbrace{1 + 2x - 1.5\,x(x - 1)}_{\text{old } p_2} + \tfrac{7}{6}\,x(x - 1)(x - 2)\)

The old part stays unchanged! You only append one term.

Check at \(x = 3\): \(1 + 6 - 1.5 \cdot 6 + \frac{7}{6} \cdot 6 = 1 + 6 - 9 + 7 = 5\) ✓
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The Newton form and divided differences
steps.insight: Newton form: a new point means just one new term. The old coefficients stay.

steps.text: Evaluating the Newton form is also efficient – with a Horner-like scheme from the inside out:
steps.explanation:
For \(p_3\) at \(x = 1.5\):
• inside: \(c_2 + (1.5 - 2) \cdot \frac{7}{6} = -1.5 - 0.5833 = -2.0833\)
• then: \(c_1 + (1.5 - 1) \cdot (-2.0833) = 2 - 1.0417 = 0.9583\)
• outside: \(c_0 + (1.5 - 0) \cdot 0.9583 = 1 + 1.4375 = 2.4375\)

This costs only about \(2n\) operations instead of \(n^2\) for Lagrange.

Note: with the fourth point the value at \(1.5\) changed from \(2.875\) to \(2.4375\). Interpolation between points is always only as good as the data describe the function.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The Newton form and divided differences
steps.insight: Evaluate the Newton form with Horner's scheme: from the inside out, \(O(n)\) operations.

steps.text: Quick check: use divided differences to compute the interpolating polynomial through \((1, 1), (2, 4), (4, 16)\).
steps.explanation:
Table:
• First differences: \(\frac{4 - 1}{2 - 1} = 3\) and \(\frac{16 - 4}{4 - 2} = 6\)
• Second difference: \(\frac{6 - 3}{4 - 1} = 1\)

\(p(x) = 1 + 3(x - 1) + 1 \cdot (x - 1)(x - 2)\)

Multiplied out: \(1 + 3x - 3 + x^2 - 3x + 2 = x^2\).

Of course: the points lie on \(y = x^2\), and the interpolating polynomial is unique. The second divided difference \(1\) is exactly \(\frac{f''}{2!} = \frac{2}{2}\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The Newton form and divided differences
steps.insight: The \(k\)-th divided difference corresponds roughly to \(\frac{f^{(k)}}{k!}\).

steps.text: If you only want to evaluate the polynomial at a single point \(x\), you do not need the coefficients at all. Neville's scheme combines interpolation values step by step:
steps.explanation:
\(P_{i,\ldots,j}\) is the value at \(x\) of the polynomial through the points \(i\) to \(j\). You start with \(P_i = y_i\) (polynomial through one point = constant) and build values for more and more points from them.

The formula is a kind of “weighted middle” of two interpolation values that share one point each.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Neville's scheme
steps.insight: Neville: compute the interpolation value at one point directly, without coefficients.

steps.text: Neville for our example at \(x = 1.5\):
steps.explanation:
Again \(2.875\) ✓

The intermediate values have a meaning: \(P_{01} = 4\) is the value of the line through the first two points at \(x = 1.5\) (extrapolation beyond \(x = 1\)). \(P_{12} = 2.5\) is the value of the line through the last two points – the linear interpolation between \(3\) and \(2\).

Neville is particularly useful for extrapolation, for example in Romberg integration (lesson “Numerical Integration”).
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Neville's scheme
steps.insight: Neville's scheme: combine row by row until a single value remains.

steps.text: Quick check: which form do you use for what?
steps.explanation:
• Writing a polynomial down once, theory, deriving formulas: Lagrange.
• Many evaluations, points added one after another: Newton with divided differences and Horner.
• Only a single value at one point, or extrapolation: Neville.
• Monomial ansatz with the Vandermonde matrix: only for very few points.

All forms describe the same polynomial – they differ only in computational cost and stability.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Neville's scheme
steps.insight: Same polynomial, different representations – the choice depends on the task.

steps.text: If the data come from a function \(f\): how far is the interpolating polynomial \(p\) from \(f\) between the nodes? The error formula gives the answer:
steps.explanation:
\(\xi\) is an (unknown) point between the nodes and \(x\).

Three factors determine the error:
• \(f^{(n+1)}\): how “smooth” is the function? If \(f\) itself is a polynomial of degree \(\le n\), this derivative is \(0\) – and so is the error.
• \((n+1)!\): grows very fast and helps.
• \(\omega(x)\): depends only on the position of the nodes. At the nodes \(\omega = 0\) (the error is zero there), in between it is not.

The formula resembles the remainder of Taylor's formula – there all nodes coincide in one point.
steps.section: Chapter 6 · How large is the error?
steps.insight: Interpolation error = \(\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!} \cdot \prod (x - x_i)\).

steps.text: An example: \(f(x) = \sin x\) is interpolated by a parabola at the nodes \(0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\).
steps.explanation:
Check: \(p(0) = 0\), \(p(\pi) = 0\), \(p\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{\pi^2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = 1\) ✓

At \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\):
• Actual error: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = 0.7071\), \(p\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{4}{\pi^2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{3\pi}{4} = 0.75\). Error \(0.043\).
• Bound: \(|f'''| = |\cos| \le 1\), \(|\omega(\frac{\pi}{4})| = \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{3\pi}{4} \approx 1.453\). So \(|f - p| \le \frac{1 \cdot 1.453}{3!} \approx 0.242\).

The bound holds, but it is pessimistic – because \(|f'''(\xi)|\) is usually smaller than its maximum.
steps.section: Chapter 6 · How large is the error?
steps.insight: Error bound: estimate \(\max |f^{(n+1)}|\), compute \(|\omega(x)|\), divide by \((n+1)!\).

steps.text: Quick check: what error do you have to expect when interpolating \(e^{x}\) on \([0, 1]\) linearly between \(x_0 = 0\) and \(x_1 = 1\)?
steps.section: Chapter 6 · How large is the error?
steps.insight: Linear interpolation: error \(\le \frac{\max|f''|}{8}\,h^2\) for node spacing \(h\).

steps.text: Natural hope: more points, higher degree – better result. The German mathematician Carl Runge showed in 1901 that this can go wrong. His function:
steps.explanation:
The animation interpolates \(f\) at equally spaced nodes:
• Degree 4: the polynomial already deviates visibly (maximum error \(0.44\)).
• Degree 8: better in the middle, but stronger oscillations at the edges (error \(1.05\)).
• Degree 14: at the edges the polynomial shoots far beyond the curve (error \(7.2\)).

More points make it worse! This is Runge's phenomenon.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Runge's phenomenon and Chebyshev nodes
steps.insight: Runge's phenomenon: with equally spaced nodes the error can explode at the edges as the degree grows.

steps.text: Why does this happen? Look at the factor \(\omega(x) = \prod (x - x_i)\) of the error formula. For equally spaced nodes it is small in the middle but huge at the edges:
steps.explanation:
In the middle of the interval every point is close to some nodes – many factors \((x - x_i)\) are small.

At the edge a point lies between two edge nodes, but far from all the others. The many large factors multiply up.

At degree 14, \(|\omega|\) at the edge is about a thousand times larger than in the middle. In addition, the higher derivatives of the Runge function grow very fast – faster than \((n+1)!\).

This is not a rounding error: even with exact arithmetic the polynomial oscillates.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Runge's phenomenon and Chebyshev nodes
steps.insight: Cause: with equally spaced nodes \(|\omega(x)|\) is much larger at the edges than in the middle.

steps.text: The solution: place the nodes more densely at the edges. Optimal are the Chebyshev nodes:
steps.explanation:
Intuitively: distribute points evenly on a semicircle and project them perpendicularly onto the diameter. At the edges they are then denser.

Example \(n = 2\) (three nodes): \(x_k = \cos\frac{\pi}{6}, \cos\frac{\pi}{2}, \cos\frac{5\pi}{6}\), i.e. \(0.866,\ 0,\ -0.866\).

For these nodes \(\max_{[-1,1]} |\omega(x)| = 2^{-n}\) – the smallest possible value. In the example: \(0.25\), compared with \(0.385\) for the equally spaced nodes \(-1, 0, 1\).

With Chebyshev nodes of degree 14 the error for the Runge function is only \(0.047\) – in the last picture of the animation you see the polynomial hugging the curve.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Runge's phenomenon and Chebyshev nodes
steps.insight: Chebyshev nodes: denser at the edges. They minimise \(\max|\omega|\) and prevent Runge's phenomenon.

steps.text: What does this mean in practice?
steps.explanation:
• Avoid high-degree polynomials through equally spaced points. Degrees up to about 4 or 5 are usually unproblematic.
• If you can choose the nodes freely: use Chebyshev nodes. Then interpolation converges very fast for smooth functions.
• If the data are given equally spaced (typical for series of measurements): interpolate piecewise – with low-degree polynomials on small subintervals. This leads to splines in the next lesson.
• Do not extrapolate: outside the range of the nodes \(\omega(x)\) grows very fast, and polynomials are completely unreliable there.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Runge's phenomenon and Chebyshev nodes
steps.insight: In practice: low degrees, Chebyshev nodes or piecewise polynomials (splines). Do not extrapolate.

steps.text: Quick check: compute the four Chebyshev nodes for \(n = 3\) on \([-1, 1]\). How do you transfer them to the interval \([0, 10]\)?
steps.explanation:
\(x_k = \cos\left(\frac{2k + 1}{8}\pi\right)\) for \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\):
• \(\cos(22.5°) \approx 0.924\)
• \(\cos(67.5°) \approx 0.383\)
• \(\cos(112.5°) \approx -0.383\)
• \(\cos(157.5°) \approx -0.924\)

On \([a, b]\) you shift and stretch linearly: \(t = \frac{a + b}{2} + \frac{b - a}{2}\,x\). For \([0, 10]\): \(t = 5 + 5x\), so \(t \approx 9.62,\ 6.91,\ 3.09,\ 0.38\).

You can see: the gaps at the edge (\(0.38\) to \(3.09\)) are smaller than in the middle (\(3.09\) to \(6.91\)).
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Runge's phenomenon and Chebyshev nodes
steps.insight: Chebyshev nodes on \([a, b]\): \(t = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{b-a}{2}\cos\left(\frac{2k+1}{2n+2}\pi\right)\).

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. For \(n + 1\) points with distinct \(x_i\) there is exactly one interpolating polynomial of degree \(\le n\).

2. Monomial ansatz: Vandermonde system – ill-conditioned for many points.

3. Lagrange: \(p = \sum y_i L_i\), \(L_i = \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j}\). Can be written down at once, good for theory.

4. Newton: \(p = c_0 + c_1(x - x_0) + \ldots\) with divided differences \(c_k = f[x_0, \ldots, x_k]\). New points = new term. Evaluation with Horner.

5. Neville: compute the value at one point directly and recursively.

6. Error: \(f - p = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\prod (x - x_i)\).

7. Runge's phenomenon for high degree and equally spaced nodes. Remedy: Chebyshev nodes or piecewise interpolation.
steps.section: Chapter 8 · Recap
steps.insight: Key message: polynomial interpolation is powerful – but only with low degree or well-chosen nodes.

steps.text: What comes next? What do you do when the data are given equally spaced and there are many points?
steps.explanation:
In the lesson “Spline Interpolation” the curve is assembled from many cubic polynomial pieces that join smoothly. This avoids Runge's phenomenon completely and produces very natural-looking curves – exactly what drawing programs and CAD systems use.

After that we use interpolating polynomials for numerical integration: Simpson's rule simply integrates the interpolating polynomial instead of the function.
steps.section: Chapter 8 · Recap
steps.insight: Next step: splines – piecewise polynomials instead of one high-degree polynomial.
